title: Throwing a yunomi in stoneware
subtitle: A tall, slightly tapered Japanese-style tea cup without a handle
excerpt: A yunomi is a Japanese everyday tea cup: taller than it is wide, slightly tapered, and held with both hands. It is an excellent throwing form for practising even wall thickness on a narrow cylinder. This tutorial covers throwing a yunomi 9 cm tall and 7 cm at the rim in smooth stoneware.
sourceNotes: Yunomi form described from standard ceramic references. No proprietary source.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Japanese-style tea cup, typically tall, slightly tapered, without a handle, and held with both hands
A narrow raised ring trimmed at the base of a wheel-thrown piece to give a finished base

content.text: is a particularly rewarding form for an intermediate thrower: it is small enough to centre easily, but its tall proportions require even upward pulling and good control of wall taper. The slight inward taper from base to rim is the characteristic yunomi silhouette. Use 250 g of stoneware.
Centre 250 g of stoneware into a compact cylinder. Open to a floor 6 mm thick. The base should be narrow: about 4 cm inside diameter.
Compress the floor with the wooden rib.
Pull the wall upward and very slightly inward so the rim is slightly narrower than the base. Aim for a wall that tapers from 7 mm at the base to 4 mm at the rim over three to four pulls.
Aim for a rim diameter of 7 cm and the height is 9 cm. The slight taper inward is the yunomi character: do not make it fully cylindrical.
Use the wooden rib on the outside to compress and refine the wall. A chamois on the rim gives a smooth finished edge.
When leather-hard, invert on the wheel and trim a

with the loop tool. The foot ring of a yunomi is traditionally narrow (about 6 mm wide) and slightly undercut on the outside to give a crisp shadow line when the cup is right-side up. Leave the inside of the foot ring base rough or lightly textured.
Make a set of four yunomi with matched dimensions for a tea service. Add a brushed iron-oxide wash to the lower half before bisque firing for a two-tone traditional look.

items.problem: Wall collapses outward at the rim during the final pull
items.cause: The wall was wetted too heavily with water during pulling, softening the clay at the rim
items.fix: Use less water on the upper half of the wall. If the rim collapses, support the outside with one finger and nudge the rim inward to restore the taper. Reduce water use on subsequent cups

items.problem: Foot ring looks off-centre when viewed from above
items.cause: The cup was not precisely centred on the wheel when inverted for trimming
items.fix: Always true-centre inverted pieces before trimming. Tap the base gently while the wheel spins slowly until the rim runs true before starting to trim
